senses.def: to have love for someone or something, based on sincere appreciation and high regard
senses.comment: Though some persons have tried to assign certain significant differences of meaning between ἀγαπάω[a], ἀγάπη[a] and φιλέω[a], φιλία (25.33), it does not seem possible to insist upon a contrast of meaning in any and all contexts. For example, the usage in John 21:15 seems to reflect simply a rhetorical alternation designed to avoid undue repetition. There is, however, one significant clue to possible meaningful differences in at least some contexts, namely, the fact that people are never commanded to love one another with φιλέω or φιλία, but only with ἀγαπάω and ἀγάπη. Though the meanings of these terms overlap considerably in many contexts, there are probably some significant differences in certain contexts; that is to say, φιλέω and φιλία are likely to focus upon love or affection based upon interpersonal association, while ἀγαπάω and ἀγάπη focus upon love and affection based on deep appreciation and high regard.

senses.def: a special type of communal meal having particular significance for early Christians as an expression of their mutual affection and concern
senses.comment: The meaning of ἀγάπη[b] may be rendered in some languages as meals in which you show your love for one another as you eat together or your eating together as the result of your love for one another.

senses.def: to hurt or to harm, with the implication of doing something which is wrong and undeserved

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to do that which is unjust or unrighteous

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to mistreat by acting unjustly toward someone
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ἀδικέω in Matthew 20:13 as to act unjustly toward (see 88.22).

senses.def: to ask for with urgency, even to the point of demanding
the son of Simon of Cyrene
a member of the high-priestly family
a Jew of Ephesus
a false teacher in the church
a coppersmith and opponent of Paul
a person in the genealogy of Jesus; compare Ἀμιναδάμ (Luke 3:33, apparatus)
to move back to a point or area from which one has previously departed, but with more explicit emphasis upon the return (compare ὑποστρέφω[a], 15.88)
senses.comment: In Luke 10:6 ἀνακάμπτω[a] occurs in a somewhat figurative context, but it is difficult to determine precisely to what extent the use of this term suggests actual movement.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἀνακάμπτω[a] to return 15.89); to turn back to a previous belief
glosses: to change to a former belief

senses.def: a person greeted in the Epistle to the Romans
to discuss, implying conflicting opinions

senses.subdomain: Hold a Wrong View, Be Mistaken
senses.def: to cause someone to have misleading or erroneous views concerning the truth
to put something away for safekeeping
glosses: to put away in a place

senses.def: to exist, with the implication of having been established and thus having continuity and purpose
senses.comment: In Colossians 1:5 the hope is the hope for reality, not a mere human feeling.

senses.def: to be necessary in view of something being inevitable
to move away from, with emphasis upon separation and possible lack of concern for what has been left
a friend of Paul
to give off or to reflect a very bright light
the state of not being subject to decay, leading to death
senses.comment: It is possible to translate this clause as ‘it will be raised and will never again die.’|In rendering ‘immortality’ it may be necessary to employ an entire clause, for example, ‘that people will not die.’ However, in 2 Timothy 1:10 ‘life and immortality’ may be best understood as a phrase in which ‘immortality’ is a qualification of ‘life,’ and therefore one may translate ‘revealing immortal life through the gospel’ or ‘revealing by means of the good news the life that does not end.’

senses.def: a continuous state or process, with the implication that the state or process in question is not interrupted by death
senses.comment: A number of scholars, however, insist that ἀφθαρσία in Ephesians 6:24 must be understood in the sense of ‘immortality’ or ‘eternity’ as a temporal expression, but one which can be rendered as ‘with undying love.’

senses.def: the family name of a certain Joseph (often called Justus) who was one of two candidates for the place of Judas Iscariot
the family name of a certain Judas who was appointed as a companion of Paul
a province in northern Asia Minor
the Aramaic name for a paved area outside the residence of Pontius Pilate and the setting for the public trial of Jesus; see 7.71
a box in which money was kept
senses.comment: It may be useful, however, in rendering John 13:29 to say simply ‘Judas had charge of the money’ or ‘Judas was the treasurer of the group,’ since the Greek expression may be understood as an idiom.

senses.def: to be able to see clearly or plainly
glosses: to be able to distinguish clearly

senses.def: to state with force and/or authority what others must do
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to order’ or ‘to command’ is ‘to speak with strength’ or ‘to speak strong words’ or, in the form of direct discourse, ‘to tell others, You must …’

senses.def: an Athenian and a member of the Areopagus who was converted by Paul
(derivative of δύναμις[a] ‘ability,’ 74.1) to be able to do or to experience something
a reference to the speaker (with an added feature of emphasis in the form ἐγώ)
senses.comment: The terminology ‘first, second, and third persons’ reflects the normal order in Greek in which the so-called first person always occurred first in any listing of participants. The second person would be in the second position, and similarly, the third person would be in a third relative position. To preserve that order in English, however, could imply impoliteness, and it is for that reason that it is preferable to translate John 10:30 as ‘the Father and I are one.’

senses.subdomain: Speaker and Those Associated with the Speaker [exclusive and inclusive]
senses.def: a reference to the speaker or writer and those associated with him or her, either including or excluding the audience (with an added feature of emphasis in the form ἡμεῖς)
to remain in a place and/or state, with expectancy concerning a future event
senses.comment: This meaning is also found as a variant reading: ἐκδεχομένων τὴν τοῦ ὕδατος κίνησιν ‘waiting for the movement of the water’ John 5:3 (apparatus).

senses.def: to expect something to happen, often implying waiting
senses.comment: The closest equivalent of ‘to expect’ is usually ‘to think that it will happen that.’

senses.def: to continue to remain in a state until an expected event

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to have departed from the patterns of correct behavior and thus to have become corrupt

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a Greek-speaking Jew in contrast to one speaking a Semitic language
senses.comment: The Greek-speaking Jews were basically Jewish in culture and religion, but they had adopted certain customs typical of the larger Greco-Roman world in which many of them lived. This inevitably resulted in certain suspicions and misunderstandings.

senses.subdomain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
senses.def: to be the object of great honor
cardinal number, where there are six instances of a countable entity
the first Christian in Asia Minor
to cause matters to be ordered in the correct manner
(derivative of ἐπίσταμαι[b] ‘to understand,’ 32.3) pertaining to being able to understand and evaluate
capacity or ability to interpret or translate
pertaining to being reverent toward God
a state of enmity with someone

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being gentle, with the implication of kindness
to cut ripe grain and to gather bundles of such grain together
an Egyptian sorcerer who together with Jannes opposed Moses before Pharaoh
a Roman centurion

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to be in a seated position

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (the Aramaic equivalent of ζηλωτής[b] and not in any way related to the geographical terms Cana or Canaan): a member of a Jewish nationalistic group seeking independence from Rome
senses.comment: It is possible that ζηλωτής in Luke 6:15 and Καναναῖος in Matthew 10:4 function not so much as a designation of an individual belonging to the particular Jewish nationalistic party (according to some scholars such a party may not have been organized at that time), but of one whjo is simply zealous for national independence (see ζηλωτής[a] ‘enthusiast, zealous person,’ 25.77). Therefore, one might speak of Simon as ‘Simon the patriot’ (the same applies to Acts 1:13, the only other occurrence of ζηλωτής[b] in the NT). To render ζηλωτής[b] as ‘armed insurrectionist’ or ‘guerilla fighter’ (as some translators have suggested) would be reading into the text more than is specifically warranted.

senses.def: to acquire, with the implication of significant effort
to attack, with the implication of gaining control over
senses.comment: The attack upon a person by a demon is often expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to ride a person,’ ‘to seize a person’s mind,’ or ‘to grab a person’s inner life.’

senses.def: to seize and take control of
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be inappropriate to translate καταλαμβάνω in John 8:3 as ‘to catch,’ since this would imply that the woman was running. A much more satisfactory rendering may be simply ‘to arrest’ or ‘to place under arrest.’

senses.def: to gain control over
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand καταλαμβάνω in John 1:5 as meaning ‘to understand’ (see 32.18).

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of καταλαμβάνω[d] ‘to overcome,’ 37.19) to come to understand something which was not understood or perceived previously
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand καταλαμβάνω in John 1:5 in the sense of ‘to overcome’ (see 37.19). In John 1:5 a word play involving both meanings may be intended, something which is typical of Johannine style.

senses.def: to acquire definite information, with the possible implication of effort
to happen to someone or something, with the implication of an event which is undesirable

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to feel contempt for someone or something because it is thought to be bad or without value
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to despise’ is ‘to think that something has no value’ or ‘to reckon something as being worthless.’

senses.def: a thin slab or bent piece of baked clay; used to cover a roof
to cause something to incline
senses.comment: See also 23.83.

senses.def: to cause to flee or run away from

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: to extend in time, with focus upon the end point
senses.comment: For another interpretation of κλίνω in Luke 9:12, see 68.51.

senses.def: to begin to come to an end, with particular reference to the period of a day (a figurative meaning dependent upon the position of the sun)
senses.comment: For another interpretation of κλίνω in Luke 9:12, see 67.118.

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.subdomain: Prostrate as an Act of Reverence or Supplication
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to incline the face to the ground) to prostrate oneself before someone as an act of reverence, fear, or supplication
(an idiom, literally: to lay down the head) to experience the rest which comes from sleep
senses.comment: ὁ δὲ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἔχει ποῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν κλίνω ‘the Son of Man has no place to lie down to rest’ Matthew 8:20, implies that Jesus possessed no permanent home. In John 19:30 this same expression must be understood not as an idiom but as a case of literally bowing the head (see 16.16).

senses.def: a Christian who sent greetings in Romans 16:23
(derivative of Κύπρος ‘Cyprus,’ 93.510) a person who is a native of Cyprus
a copper (or bronze) coin worth 1/2 of a quadrans or 1/128 of a denarius
senses.comment: In practically all instances, references to ἀσσάριον (6.77), κοδράντης (6.78), or λεπτόν may be made in terms of ‘a very small coin’ or ‘a coin with very little value’ or ‘money that was not worth very much.’

senses.def: to dissolve the marriage bond
senses.comment: Expressions for divorce are often based on terms meaning literally ‘to send away,’ ‘to separate from,’ or ‘to leave one another.’ However, in a number of languages idiomatic expressions are employed, for example ‘to send him off with his clothes,’ ‘to untie the knot between them,’ or ‘to throw away her hearthstones.’|Some persons have attempted to make an important distinction between ἀφίημι in 1 Corinthians 7:11 and χωρίζω in 1 Corinthians 7:15 on the assumption that ἀφίημι implies legal divorce, while χωρίζω only relates to separation. Such a distinction, however, seems to be quite artificial.

senses.def: the mother of Jesus Christ
a sister of Martha and Lazarus[a]
Mary Magdalene, a follower of Jesus
the mother of James[d] and Joseph[g]
the wife of Clopas
the mother of John Mark
a person greeted in Romans 16:6
part or portion, with the possible implication of a division or significant distinction
an administrative district
senses.comment: In Acts 16:12 (the only occurrence of μερίς[b] in the NT) the Greek New Testament published by the United Bible Societies has adopted a conjectural emendation, since the more traditional text, πρώτη τῆς μερίδος, literally ‘first of the district,’ is not only misleading in meaning but does not reflect the historical fact that Philippi was a city in one of the four districts of Macedonia but was not a capital city.

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: a period of time measured by a complete cycle in the phases of the moon
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘month’ is simply ‘moon,’ so that one would translate this expression in Luke 1:24 as ‘she kept herself in seclusion for five moons.’

senses.def: hard work, implying unusual exertion of energy and effort
to be or to become like a child
to receive and show hospitality to a stranger, that is, someone who is not regarded as a member of the extended family or a close friend
glosses: to receive a stranger as a guest
senses.comment: To receive a stranger as a guest is sometimes expressed idiomatically as ‘to let a stranger sit at one’s table,’ ‘to offer a bed to a stranger,’ or ‘to let a stranger enter one’s house.’

senses.def: (compare ξένος ‘unknown, surprising,’ 28.34) to experience a sudden feeling of unexpected wonder
senses.comment: The experience of ‘surprise’ may be expressed idiomatically in some languages, for example, ‘to be left with one’s mouth open’ or ‘to have one’s eyes made wide open.’

senses.def: a relatively small quantity on any dimension
a relatively low point on a scale of extent
senses.comment: The first ὀλίγον in Luke 7:47 is an expression of quantity (see 59.13), while the second ὀλίγον indicates degree. Accordingly, in some languages it may be necessary to translate Luke 7:47 as ‘but whoever has been forgiven only a few things loves only a little bit.’|In a number of languages, however, it is impossible to speak of ‘not a little’ (a case of litotes or purposeful understatement). The appropriate equivalent in Acts 12:18 would be simply ‘there was great confusion among the guards’ or ‘the guards were intensely disturbed’ or ‘the guards were in tremendous confusion.’

senses.def: a relatively small quantity

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a relatively brief extent of time
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret ἐν ὀλίγῳ in Acts 26:28 as meaning ‘easily’ or ‘without difficulty’ (see 22.41).|In some languages it may be best to translate the phrase in 1 Peter 5:12 as ‘I have written a brief letter.’

senses.def: the mature fruit of plants (that is, fruit which is ready for use)
senses.comment: In this one occurrence of ὀπώρα in the NT, ‘ripe fruit’ is to be understood in a figurative sense of ‘good things.’

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: tail of an animal or insect
senses.comment: In some languages it may be important to distinguish clearly between the tail of a mammal, a fish, and a creature such as the scorpion.

senses.def: all possible positions
pertaining to being marked with a sign
senses.comment: In Acts 28:11 the reference is to the images of the Dioscuri, ‘the twin gods,’ carved on the prow of the ship. For παράσημον as a noun, see παράσημος[b] 6.51.

senses.def: an identifying emblem, possibly a carved figurehead at the prow of a ship
senses.comment: In translating the expression ‘emblem of the Twin Gods’ it may be possible to use a phrase such as ‘a carving of the Twin Gods’ or ‘a statue of the Twin Gods.’ For παράσημος as an adjective, see 33.479.

senses.def: persons of successive generations who are related by birth
senses.comment: In biblical times the reckoning of a lineage was somewhat complex in view of certain distinctions between legal and biological relations. The focus of meaning in γένεσις[b], οἶκος[c], and πατριά[a] is not, however, the list of ancestors, but the lineage of successively related persons to which the reference person belongs. Some scholars, however, interpret γένεσις[c] history, 33.19).|In some languages a successive series of ancestors is called ‘the forefathers’ or ‘those to whom one looks back’ or ‘those who have gone ahead.’ In other languages a lineage is referred to as ‘a person’s root’ or ‘a man’s trunk’ (referring to the trunk of a tree).|In Luke 2:4 there appears to be no significant difference in meaning between οἶκος and πατριά, and in some receptor languages it would be sufficient to use a single term essentially equivalent to ‘lineage.’ The two terms appear to simply reinforce their shared meaning.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a relatively large unit of people who constitute a sociopolitical group, sharing a presumed biological descent (in many contexts πατριά[b] and φυλή[b] are very similar in meaning to ἔθνος and λαός[a], 11.55)

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to stand around someone or to encircle
to keep oneself away from being involved in some activity
pertaining to being bitter or pungent

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of πικρός[a] ‘bitter,’ 79.41) pertaining to feeling resentful
to apply pressure around the neck in order to harm or kill
(figurative extension of meaning employing the base πνίγω[a] ‘to choke,’ 19.53) to cause the death of plants by other plants crowding them out and/or overshadowing them
to die as the result of drowning ‎
a marker of an indirect condition

senses.subdomain: Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
senses.def: pertaining to being eager to do something
senses.comment: It would be wrong to equate the meaning of πρόθυμος and προθύμως with ἑκούσιος, ἑκών, and ἑκουσίως (25.65), for πρόθυμος and προθύμως imply far more desire and eagerness, though both sets of terms are often translated in English as ‘willing’ or ‘willingly.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a decided and unjustified preference for something or someone
first in a series involving time, space, or set
senses.comment: In Hebrews 9:2 πρῶτος must be understood in the sense of the outer tent, which was the first one to which a person came in entering the sanctuary.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: pertaining to a point of time earlier in a sequence

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: pertaining to being of high rank, with the implication of special prominence and status
pertaining to being superior in value to all other items of the same class
pertaining to exceeding everything else in importance
senses.comment: In some languages ‘most important’ is expressed by a negative comparison, for example, ‘the commandment that nothing else surpasses’ or ‘the commandment than which nothing else is greater’ or ‘… of more value.’

senses.subdomain: Application and Removal of Liquids or Masses
senses.def: to sprinkle a liquid upon something
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be important to restructure somewhat this elliptical phrase in 1 Peter 1:2 so as to translate ‘to obey Jesus Christ and be sprinkled by his blood’ or ‘… be purified by his blood.’

senses.def: a Galilean woman who followed Jesus
(derivative of Σιδών ‘Sidon,’ 93.577) pertaining to Sidon
(derivative of Σιδών ‘Sidon,’ 93.577) a person who lives in or is a native of Sidon
a state of firm, inner strength

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to be bent over in a doubled up position
coming to an agreement with, often implying a type of joint decision
(derivative of συνοδεύω ‘to travel with,’ 15.149) a group of persons travelling together
glosses: a group of those travelling with

senses.def: a Christian in Beroea
to bring an activity to a successful finish

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
senses.def: (derivative of τέλος[a] ‘end,’ 67.66) to occur or happen at the end of a duration
to cause to happen for some end result
to obey as a means of fulfilling the purpose of a rule or standard
senses.comment: The phrase ‘to obey the Law’ in Romans 2:27 may be rendered simply as ‘to do what the Law says one must do.’

senses.def: to pay tax or tribute (used absolutely or with a noun complement meaning ‘tax’ or ‘tribute’)

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time subsequent to another point of time
pertaining to being the color of the flower hyacinth (see 2.41), probably a shade of blue
senses.comment: Since in some languages the flower hyacinth may not be as well known as precious stones such as sapphire and turquoise, it may be possible to render Revelation 9:17 as ‘blue as sapphire’ or ‘blue as turquoise.’ The justification for this is simply that the Greek term ὑακίνθινος had become primarily a designation for color.

senses.def: (derivative of ὑπηρετέω[a] ‘to serve,’ 35.19) a person who renders service
senses.comment: In rendering θεράπων, ὑπηρέτης, and διάκονος[a] in the sense of ‘servant,’ it is important to avoid a term which would be too specific, for example, ‘one who serves meals’ or ‘one who works around the house.’ It may, in fact, be necessary to use an expression which means essentially ‘helper.’|In the NT ὑπηρέτης is employed to refer to many diverse types of servants, such as attendants to a king, officers of the Sanhedrin, attendants of magistrates, and, especially in the Gospel of John, Jewish Temple guards.

senses.def: to cause to become visible
senses.comment: In a number of languages the meaning of ‘appeared to’ must be expressed as two closely related events, so that in John 21:1 it may be necessary to translate ‘Jesus came and was seen once more by his disciples’ or ‘Jesus came and once more his disciples saw him.’

senses.def: to cause something to be fully known by revealing clearly and in some detail
a male person with whom one associates and for whom there is affection or personal regard
senses.comment: In some languages there are different terms for different grades of friends, that is to say, a difference between intimate friends with whom one constantly shares and those who constitute a somewhat wider circle of persons who are on friendly terms but who are not in the inner circle of intimate relations. The choice of terms for ‘friend’ will depend, of course, upon individual contexts.

senses.def: a female person with whom one associates and for whom there is affection or personal regard
senses.comment: See discussion at 34.11.

senses.def: any kind of plant, whether tree, bush, or herb
senses.comment: The principal translational difficulty with φυτεία is that in so many languages there is no term with such a generic meaning. Sometimes the closest equivalent is a descriptive phrase ‘green things’ or ‘leafy things.’|Classifications of plants vary greatly from one language to another. Principal distinctions are based upon size, woodiness, perennials versus annuals, and food-producing in contrast with non-food-producing.

senses.def: (derivative of χοῦς ‘dust,’ 2.15) pertaining to being made or consisting of dust or soil
senses.comment: Though in general χοῦς and the derivative χοϊκός would seem to refer to dry dust, they may also refer to dirt or soil. In 1 Corinthians 15:47 it is more appropriate to speak of the creation of Adam as ‘made from the ground’ or ‘formed out of soil.’ For another interpretation of χοϊκός in 1 Corinthians 15:47, see 1.42.

senses.def: pertaining to having the nature of earthly existence in contrast with that which is heavenly or of heaven
senses.comment: It may even be possible in rendering χοϊκός in 1 Corinthians 15:47 to say ‘created out of earth’ or ‘made from dust’ (see 2.16).

senses.def: (derivative of ψεύδομαι ‘to lie,’ 33.253) the content of a false utterance
senses.comment: It may be important in some instances to restructure the semantic relationships in this clause in Romans 3:7, for example, ‘if my lie makes God’s truth appear more glorious.’
